facts: Never a blood culture contaminant: S. aureus bacteraemia needs echo, repeat cultures, source control and infection specialist review.
Skin and soft tissue, bone and joint, line, device and endovascular infection.
PVL-producing strains cause recurrent boils and necrotising pneumonia (send for PVL testing).
orgs.tx: Flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 6 hours (every 4 hours for endocarditis), or cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours.
orgs.alt: Penicillin allergy: vancomycin or teicoplanin (inferior to β-lactams for MSSA). Oral options by susceptibility: doxycycline, co-trimoxazole, clindamycin, linezolid; rifampicin only in combination for prosthetic material.

facts: Resistant to all β-lactams except ceftaroline and ceftobiprole (mecA/mecC).
Decolonisation (nasal mupirocin and skin wash) before surgery and for recurrent infection.
Contact precautions per local IPC policy.
orgs.tx: Vancomycin (AUC-guided) or teicoplanin IV for serious infection; daptomycin for bacteraemia or endocarditis (specialist).
orgs.alt: Oral by susceptibility: doxycycline, co-trimoxazole, linezolid, clindamycin (check D-test). Ceftaroline for salvage.

orgs.syn: cons staph epidermidis coag negative staphylococcus epidermidis haemolyticus hominis capitis
facts: Commonest blood culture contaminant: a single positive set without prosthetic material usually needs no treatment.
Real pathogens on lines, prosthetic valves, devices, joints and shunts (biofilm).
Most hospital isolates are methicillin resistant.
orgs.tx: If significant: vancomycin or teicoplanin, and remove the infected line or device where possible.
orgs.alt: Line kept: 10–14 days with antibiotic lock. Prosthetic joint or valve: specialist regimens, often with rifampicin.

facts: Coagulase negative, but behaves like S. aureus: aggressive native valve endocarditis and abscesses.
Typical endocarditis organism in the Duke-ISCVID criteria.
orgs.tx: Treat as S. aureus: flucloxacillin or cefazolin if susceptible (many are also penicillin susceptible).
orgs.alt: Echocardiography for all bacteraemias.

orgs.syn: gas group a strep igas scarlet fever necrotising fasciitis toxic shock
facts: Pharyngitis, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, streptococcal toxic shock, puerperal sepsis.
Invasive disease is notifiable; high-risk household contacts need prophylaxis.
Always penicillin susceptible; macrolide and clindamycin resistance about 5–15%.
orgs.tx: Benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours; add clindamycin 1.2 g IV every 6 hours for necrotising infection or toxic shock.
orgs.alt: Consider IVIG in streptococcal toxic shock. Urgent surgical review for necrotising fasciitis.

facts: Neonatal sepsis and meningitis; maternal colonisation guides intrapartum prophylaxis.
In adults: diabetes, malignancy, older age; skin, bone, joint and endocarditis.
orgs.tx: Benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours (or amoxicillin).
orgs.alt: Clindamycin resistance is common (about 30%): not reliable as an alternative without susceptibility results.

facts: Pneumonia, meningitis, otitis, sinusitis and bacteraemia.
Penicillin resistance is uncommon in the UK but common in many other countries.
Urinary antigen test helps in pneumonia.
orgs.tx: Pneumonia: amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin. Meningitis: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours with dexamethasone (benzylpenicillin if MIC ≤ 0.06).
orgs.alt: Doxycycline or a macrolide for non-severe pneumonia in penicillin allergy; levofloxacin for severe allergy.

orgs.syn: vgs strep mitis oralis sanguinis salivarius mutans
facts: Oral flora; typical endocarditis organisms.
Severe sepsis in neutropenia with mucositis.
A single blood culture set may be a contaminant.
orgs.tx: Benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone, guided by the penicillin MIC (see the endocarditis guide for endocarditis regimens).
orgs.alt: Penicillin allergy: vancomycin or teicoplanin.

facts: Abscess formers: brain, liver, lung, dental, intra-abdominal.
Bacteraemia should prompt imaging for an abscess.
orgs.tx: Benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone plus drainage of any collection; add metronidazole for mixed abscesses.
orgs.alt: Brain abscess: ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, 6–8 weeks.

facts: Urinary, biliary, intra-abdominal and line infection; typical endocarditis organism.
Intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; low-level aminoglycoside resistance.
Usually amoxicillin susceptible.
orgs.tx: Amoxicillin 2 g IV every 4–6 hours. Endocarditis: amoxicillin plus ceftriaxone, or amoxicillin plus gentamicin if no high-level resistance.
orgs.alt: Penicillin allergy: vancomycin or teicoplanin. Lower UTI: nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin.

orgs.syn: enterococcus faecium vre vancomycin-resistant enterococci gre
facts: Mostly hospital-acquired, after broad-spectrum antibiotics; usually amoxicillin resistant.
VRE (VanA or VanB) colonises the gut; contact precautions.
Intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins.
orgs.tx: Vancomycin or teicoplanin if susceptible. VRE: linezolid or daptomycin (high dose, specialist).
orgs.alt: Lower UTI with VRE: nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin. VanB strains may be teicoplanin susceptible.

facts: Meningitis, rhombencephalitis and bacteraemia in pregnancy, older age, immunosuppression and alcohol excess.
Foodborne (soft cheese, pâté, deli meat).
Intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins.
orgs.tx: Amoxicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours, plus gentamicin for the first 7 days in CNS infection; 21 days for meningitis.
orgs.alt: Penicillin allergy: co-trimoxazole. Add amoxicillin to empirical meningitis treatment when Listeria is possible.

orgs.syn: c diff c. diff cdi clostridium difficile
facts: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and colitis; toxin testing confirms infection, PCR alone may be carriage.
Highest risk with clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and quinolones.
Isolate with enteric precautions; alcohol gel does not kill spores.
orgs.tx: Oral vancomycin 125 mg every 6 hours for 10 days, or fidaxomicin 200 mg every 12 hours for 10 days.
orgs.alt: Recurrence: fidaxomicin; consider faecal microbiota transplant after multiple recurrences. See the C. difficile guide.

facts: Gas gangrene, necrotising soft tissue infection, biliary and gut sepsis; massive haemolysis with C. perfringens bacteraemia.
C. septicum bacteraemia: look for colorectal or haematological malignancy.
orgs.tx: Benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin, with urgent surgical debridement.
orgs.alt: Metronidazole or co-amoxiclav for mixed intra-abdominal infection.

facts: Commonest cause of UTI and Gram-negative bacteraemia; biliary and intra-abdominal infection.
UK resistance: amoxicillin about 50–60%, trimethoprim about 30%, co-amoxiclav 20–40%; ESBL about 10–15% of bacteraemias.
STEC (O157): do not give antibiotics (risk of HUS).
orgs.tx: Narrow by susceptibility; bacteraemia commonly treated with ceftriaxone or co-amoxiclav, then oral step-down, 7 days total if uncomplicated.
orgs.alt: Lower UTI: nitrofurantoin, pivmecillinam or fosfomycin. ESBL: see the Gram-negative bacteraemia guide.

facts: UTI, pneumonia, biliary and line infection; hypervirulent strains cause liver abscess with metastatic spread (eye, CNS).
Intrinsically resistant to amoxicillin.
A common host for ESBL and carbapenemase genes.
orgs.tx: Ceftriaxone or a carbapenem by susceptibility (ESBL: meropenem).
orgs.alt: Liver abscess: drain and treat 4–6 weeks; check eyes in hypervirulent infection.

facts: High-risk chromosomal AmpC: third-generation cephalosporins and piperacillin–tazobactam can fail on treatment.
Hospital-acquired pneumonia, line, surgical site and urinary infection.
orgs.tx: Cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours if MIC ≤ 2 mg/L, otherwise a carbapenem.
orgs.alt: Oral step-down by susceptibility: ciprofloxacin or co-trimoxazole.

facts: Formerly Enterobacter aerogenes; high-risk chromosomal AmpC.
orgs.tx: Cefepime if MIC ≤ 2 mg/L, otherwise a carbapenem.
orgs.alt: Avoid ceftriaxone and piperacillin–tazobactam for serious infection.

facts: High-risk chromosomal AmpC. C. koseri (no inducible AmpC) causes neonatal brain abscess.
orgs.tx: Cefepime if MIC ≤ 2 mg/L, otherwise a carbapenem.
orgs.alt: Avoid ceftriaxone and piperacillin–tazobactam for serious infection.

facts: Hospital outbreaks (neonatal units), line and respiratory infection; typical endocarditis organism with prosthetic material.
Low-risk chromosomal AmpC; intrinsically resistant to colistin and nitrofurantoin.
orgs.tx: Treat by susceptibility (ceftriaxone or cefepime if susceptible).
orgs.alt: Ciprofloxacin or co-trimoxazole orally if susceptible.

facts: UTI, catheter blockage and struvite stones (urease).
Intrinsically resistant to colistin, nitrofurantoin and tetracyclines (including tigecycline).
orgs.tx: Amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone by susceptibility.
orgs.alt: Do not use nitrofurantoin.

facts: Catheter-associated UTI in long-term care; low-risk chromosomal AmpC.
Intrinsically resistant to colistin, nitrofurantoin and tetracyclines.
orgs.tx: Treat by susceptibility (ceftriaxone or cefepime if susceptible).
orgs.alt: Change the catheter.

facts: Gastroenteritis: usually no antibiotics.
Treat if bacteraemic, very young or old, immunosuppressed, or with prosthetic or vascular grafts (endovascular infection risk).
Notifiable (food poisoning).
orgs.tx: Invasive disease: ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, then ciprofloxacin or azithromycin by susceptibility.
orgs.alt: Bacteraemia over 50: consider vascular imaging for endovascular infection.

facts: Enteric fever after travel, mostly South Asia; fever, headache, abdominal pain, relative bradycardia.
Most South Asian isolates are ciprofloxacin resistant; XDR Typhi from Pakistan is resistant to ceftriaxone.
Notifiable; food handlers and children need exclusion and clearance.
orgs.tx: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily then oral azithromycin; meropenem for XDR or severe disease.
orgs.alt: Usual total 7–14 days.

facts: Hospital-acquired pneumonia, ventilator, burns, cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis, urinary catheter and line infection, otitis externa.
Intrinsically resistant to amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, ceftriaxone, ertapenem, trimethoprim and tetracyclines.
Typical endocarditis organism with prosthetic material.
orgs.tx: Piperacillin–tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime or meropenem by susceptibility (extended infusions in critical illness).
orgs.alt: Oral: ciprofloxacin 750 mg every 12 hours. Difficult-to-treat: ceftolozane–tazobactam or ceftazidime–avibactam.

facts: ICU, ventilator, burns and wound infection; survives on surfaces (outbreaks).
Carbapenem-resistant strains (CRAB) are common in many countries.
Distinguish colonisation from infection.
orgs.tx: Carbapenem if susceptible; carbapenem-resistant strains need microbiology advice (sulbactam-based regimens, colistin combinations).
orgs.alt: Remove infected lines. Tigecycline is unsuitable for bacteraemia.

facts: Opportunist after carbapenems, in ventilated, neutropenic or line-dependent patients; often colonisation in sputum.
Intrinsically resistant to carbapenems and aminoglycosides.
orgs.tx: High-dose co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim 8–12 mg/kg/day), often initially combined with minocycline, levofloxacin or cefiderocol.
orgs.alt: Ceftazidime–avibactam plus aztreonam. Remove infected lines.

facts: Cystic fibrosis (cepacia syndrome) and chronic granulomatous disease; contaminated products in outbreaks.
Intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides and colistin.
orgs.tx: Specialist advice; options include co-trimoxazole, meropenem or ceftazidime by susceptibility.
orgs.alt: B. pseudomallei (melioidosis) is a different organism: inform the laboratory (hazard group 3).

facts: COPD exacerbation, pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis; invasive non-typeable disease in adults and neonates.
Type b (Hib) is rare since vaccination; contacts may need rifampicin.
About 15–20% produce β-lactamase.
orgs.tx: Amoxicillin if β-lactamase negative; co-amoxiclav, doxycycline or ceftriaxone otherwise.
orgs.alt: Meningitis: ceftriaxone for 10 days.

facts: Otitis, sinusitis and COPD exacerbations.
Over 90% produce β-lactamase: amoxicillin is unreliable.
orgs.tx: Co-amoxiclav, doxycycline or clarithromycin.

facts: Meningitis and septicaemia with a non-blanching rash; notify immediately.
Close contacts need ciprofloxacin; serogroup A, C, W or Y contacts also need MenACWY.
Recurrent disease: test for complement deficiency.
orgs.tx: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours for 5 days (benzylpenicillin if susceptible).
orgs.alt: Index case: ciprofloxacin before discharge if not treated with ceftriaxone.

facts: Urethritis, cervicitis, pharyngeal and rectal infection; disseminated gonococcal infection (arthritis, rash).
Ceftriaxone-resistant strains are rising: always culture before treatment and test of cure.
Refer to sexual health for partner notification.
orgs.tx: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose (BASHH).
orgs.alt: If susceptibility known: ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally single dose. Disseminated infection: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily.

facts: Commonest bacterial gastroenteritis in the UK (poultry); Guillain–Barré syndrome afterwards.
Quinolone resistance is common.
orgs.tx: Usually no antibiotics. If severe, immunosuppressed or prolonged: clarithromycin or azithromycin.

facts: Intra-abdominal abscess, peritonitis, diabetic foot and pelvic infection; usually mixed with gut organisms.
Clindamycin resistance is common; metronidazole and carbapenem resistance are emerging.
orgs.tx: Metronidazole, co-amoxiclav or piperacillin–tazobactam, with drainage.
orgs.alt: Bacteraemia: look for an abscess or perforation.

facts: Severe pneumonia with confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia; hotels, cruises, spas, cooling towers.
Urinary antigen detects serogroup 1 only: send respiratory PCR or culture.
Notifiable.
orgs.tx: Clarithromycin or levofloxacin (levofloxacin preferred if severe).
orgs.alt: Usually 7–10 days; longer if immunosuppressed.

facts: Pneumonia in young adults, epidemics every few years; cold agglutinins, rash, encephalitis.
No cell wall: β-lactams are inactive.
Macrolide resistance is rising in some regions.
orgs.tx: Doxycycline or clarithromycin.
orgs.alt: Levofloxacin for macrolide-resistant or severe infection.

facts: Commonest cause of candidaemia; usually fluconazole susceptible.
Remove central lines, repeat cultures daily, fundoscopy and echo as indicated.
orgs.tx: Echinocandin first, step down to fluconazole when stable and cleared.
orgs.alt: 14 days from first negative culture if uncomplicated.

facts: Reduced azole susceptibility; echinocandin resistance (FKS) in about 5–10%.
orgs.tx: Echinocandin; step down only if fluconazole (high dose) or voriconazole susceptible.
orgs.alt: Liposomal amphotericin B if resistant to both.

facts: Multi-resistant yeast that spreads in hospitals; contact precautions and screening of contacts.
Most isolates are fluconazole resistant.
orgs.tx: Echinocandin; liposomal amphotericin B if resistant or failing.
orgs.alt: Do not treat colonisation. Inform IPC and UKHSA.

facts: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in neutropenia, transplant, ICU (influenza, COVID-19) and high-dose steroids.
Azole resistance (TR34/L98H) is rising: request susceptibility testing.
orgs.tx: Voriconazole or isavuconazole.
orgs.alt: Liposomal amphotericin B if azole resistant or unsuitable.

facts: Meningitis in advanced HIV, transplant and other immunosuppression; raised intracranial pressure is common.
Serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen.
orgs.tx: Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction, then fluconazole.
orgs.alt: Therapeutic LPs for raised pressure; delay ART 4–6 weeks.
